description: Core Dev 5 is a team of five students from Kano: three software engineering students and two cybersecurity students, one of whom is our UI/UX designer. We are building a browser game that teaches kids aged 7 to 12 how astronauts balance power, air, food and radiation on a Moon or Mars base, using live NASA DONKI solar flare data so every mission reflects the real Sun.
summary: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a free browser game where kids aged 7 to 12 command a base on the Moon or Mars for 10 days. Every day they split a limited supply of power between life support, a greenhouse, a radiation shield and a science lab, so every choice has a cost. https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1ZM4hlGHTEUcTsYgW3fp0UirgHOGwD_np/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=107503788876083194596&rtpof=true&sd=trueReal solar flares from NASA's DONKI space weather database strike the base, and on Mars, warnings from Earth can arrive too late because messages take minutes to travel. Kids learn three true lessons about deep space: power is limited, radiation is a real danger, and astronauts far from Earth must sometimes decide alone. It runs on any phone or laptop with no download and no login.
details:
What it does

The player is the commander of a base at Peak Near Shackleton on the Moon (one of NASA's Artemis III candidate landing regions) or at Jezero crater on Mars. Each day, CAPCOM Kemi from Mission Control reads the morning news. The player then shares out that day's power using simple plus and minus buttons. Life support makes air, the greenhouse grows food, the shield blocks radiation and the lab earns science points. Forecasts show what will happen before the day runs, and warnings appear if air or food is heading toward zero. After each day, a report explains in plain words why things changed.

How it teaches real trade-offs

There is never enough power for everything, so no choice is free. Putting power into the shield on a flare day protects the crew but costs science. Skipping life support saves power today but uses up air reserves. The Moon and Mars need different strategies: the Moon has more sunlight but more radiation, while Mars has dust storms and a message delay of about 3 to 22 minutes, so half of all flare warnings arrive after the flare. Kids learn to keep some shielding on every sol and to plan without waiting for Earth.

Replayability and learning from failure

Events are random each time. Missions end with up to three stars, specific tips based on what went wrong, and six badges to collect, such as Flare Survivor for blocking a whole solar flare. If a mission fails, the crew always flies home safely, so failure feels like a lesson, not a punishment.

How we built it

The game is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no backend, no accounts and no tracking. It is hosted on GitHub Pages. The game rules are separated from the screen code and covered by 53 automated tests. Every science word is explained in context, buttons are large enough for small hands, and the game can be played with a keyboard.

Reliability

During the hackathon, NASA's api.nasa.gov flare feed returned errors. We built a three-step fallback: the game asks NASA's CCMC DONKI service first, then api.nasa.gov, then uses an archive of 34 real flares from March 2025. Every flare is labelled LIVE or ARCHIVED, so stored data is never shown as live.

Real NASA science inside the game

Each day offers an experiment card based on one of 8 real NASA Open Science Data Repository studies, such as lettuce grown in Veggie on the ISS (OSD-267) and plants grown in Apollo Moon soil (OSD-476). Every day report ends with a real science fact and its source. The results screen compares the crew's radiation with one week of real ISS measurements from NASA RadLab (DosTel1 detector, Columbus module, about 209 microgray a day).

What's next

Cadet and Commander difficulty levels and a classroom mode for teachers.
